1:1: אֵיכָה ׀ יָשְׁבָה בָדָד הָעִיר רַבָּתִי עָם

The author is speaking of the city of Jerusalem as if it were a woman who could sit alone in mourning. See the Introduction to Lamentations for further discussion of the term and how to translate it here and throughout this book.
The point of this comparison is that just as a widow is alone, unprotected, and grieving, so is Jerusalem now without allies or support.
Here the author is speaking as if Jerusalem were a princess who has been reduced to slavery.
1:2: בָּכוֹ תִבְכֶּה בַּלַּיְלָה וְדִמְעָתָהּ עַל לֶחֱיָהּ
The author is speaking of the city of Jerusalem as if it were a woman who weeps and has tears on her cheeks. See the note on verse one.
כָּל־רֵעֶיהָ בָּגְדוּ בָהּ הָיוּ לָהּ לְאֹיְבִים
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
1:3: The author is speaking of having a secure and peaceful home as if it were a resting place that Judah could find.
Here the author is speaking as if being trapped with no escape were being caught between the narrow passes of a mountain gorge.
1:4: The author is speaking of the roads of Zion as if they were a person who could mourn. He means that the roads are empty and unused.
1:5: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
1:6: The author is speaking of Jerusalem and its people as if the city were a daughter.
Here the author is speaking as if Jerusalem’s majesty were a person or thing that could depart from her.
The point of this comparison is that just as deer that have found no pasture are weak and helpless, so are Her princes without strength or resources.
1:8: Here the author is speaking as if Jerusalem were an object of ritual abhorrence, something that people treat as defiling and avoid.
By her nakedness, the author means her naked body is being exposed to shame before her enemies.
Turning backward was a symbolic action by which Jerusalem showed her shame and disgrace before those who saw her.
1:9: The author is referring to menstrual impurity in a polite way by using the phrase Her uncleanness is in her skirts. He uses this image to characterize Jerusalem’s profound defilement before God.
The author is speaking of Jerusalem’s ruin as if she were going down to a lower place.
The word himself indicates that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb.
1:11: The author is using one kind of food, bread, to mean food in general.
1:12: Jerusalem is speaking to all you who pass along the way, people who are not in conversation with her. She is doing this to communicate to the people listening to her that she feels very strongly about her suffering. It would be good to present verse12 through verse16 as a direct quotation, if possible, to show that Jerusalem is speaking to the people.
Jerusalem is using the question form to emphasize that the passers–by should pay attention to its suffering and that no one has ever suffered as it has.
The speaker is using the day of his burning anger as a common expression of the culture to mean the time when the Lord expressed his fierce anger in judgment.
1:13: Jerusalem is speaking as if God’s judgment were fire that he sent from heaven into her bones and that ruled over them.
Here Jerusalem is speaking as if God were a hunter who spread a net to catch prey and turned her back so she could not escape.
1:14: נִשְׂקַד עֹל פְּשָׁעַי בְּיָדוֹ יִשְׂתָּרְגוּ עָלוּ עַל־צַוָּארִי
Here Jerusalem is speaking as if her sins were a yoke that was bound fast and intertwined and placed on her neck, like the wooden frame placed on the neck of a draft animal to control it.
1:15: Here Jerusalem is speaking as if the Lord were a person who has trodden the winepress, crushing grapes underfoot. She means that the Lord has crushed the people of Judah in judgment.
Jerusalem is speaking of the people of Judah as if they were a virgin daughter.
1:16: אֲנִי בוֹכִיָּה עֵינִי ׀ עֵינִי יֹרְדָה מַּיִם
The repetition of the phrases, I, I am weeping and my eye, my eye is an emphatic form. Jerusalem is using the repetition for emphasis to express the intensity of her weeping.
Here Jerusalem is speaking as if her eye were a stream of water running down.
Jerusalem is speaking of her life as if it were something that could be restored and given back to her.
1:17: The author is speaking of Zion as if it were a woman who could spread out her hands in a gesture of pleading.
Here the author is speaking as if Jerusalem were an object of ritual abhorrence, something that the surrounding nations treat as defiling and avoid. See the note on verse 8.
1:18: צַדִּיק הוּא יְהוָה כִּי פִיהוּ מָרִיתִי

It would be good to present verse18 through verse22 as a direct quotation, if possible, to show that the city of Jerusalem is speaking. In, Jerusalem speaks to passers–by, and in she speaks directly to the Lord.
Jerusalem is speaking to all peoples. She is doing this to communicate to the people listening that she feels very strongly about her suffering.
1:19: The repetition of the pronoun they, they is an emphatic form. Jerusalem is using the repetition for emphasis to express the depth of betrayal.
Jerusalem is referring to death in a polite way by using the word expired.
1:20: Here, my inward parts represent deep emotions.
Here Jerusalem is speaking as if her heart had been physically overturned within her. She means that she is in complete emotional anguish.
Jerusalem is referring to all of the destruction by naming two extremes, Outside and inside.
1:21: When Jerusalem says and let them be like me, she is saying what she wants God to do.
2:1: The writer is speaking of the Lord bringing judgment on Jerusalem as if the Lord covered with a cloud the city, that is, as if he brought darkness and gloom upon it.
The writer is using the phrase in his nose as a common expression of the culture to mean that the Lord is angry.

The writer is speaking of the people of Jerusalem as if they were a daughter of the city. This is a common expression in the original language for referring to a city and its inhabitants. See the Lamentations 2 Introduction for more information.

The writer is speaking of the Lord removing Israel’s honor as if the Lord had cast down from heaven to earth the splendor of Israel. The image of heaven represents a high and honored position, while earth represents a low and disgraced position.
Here, the footstool of his feet represents the temple in Jerusalem, since the temple was considered the place where God’s presence rested on earth, as a king rests his feet on a footstool.
Here, on the day of his nose represents the time or occasion when God acted in judgment.
2:2: The writer is speaking of the Lord completely destroying the settlements of Jacob as if the Lord has swallowed them up, as a person might consume food.
Here, all the pastures of Jacob represents the dwelling places of the people of Israel, since pastures were the places where people lived and kept their flocks.
The writer is speaking of the Lord destroying the fortifications as if he has brought them to the ground, that is, knocked them flat.
The writer is speaking of the Lord stripping the kingdom and its rulers of their honor and dignity as if they were sacred things that the Lord had made common and unclean.
2:3: גָּדַע בָּחֳרִי אַף כֹּל קֶרֶן יִשְׂרָאֵל
The writer is speaking of God removing the power of Israel as if God cut off every horn, since a horn represents the strength and power of an animal.
Here, nose represents the emotion of wrath, since the nostrils flare when a person is angry.

Here, his right hand represents God’s power to help and protect his people, since the right hand was associated with strength and action. The writer says that God turned back this power, meaning he withdrew his protection.

Jeremiah is using from the face of as a common expression to mean “from before” or “away from the direction of.” He means that God withdrew his right hand away from facing the enemy, leaving Israel unprotected.
The writer uses this comparison to say that God’s judgment was as destructive to Israel as a fire of flame is to whatever it burns.
The writer is continuing the image of fire, speaking of God’s judgment as a flame that destroys everything in its path. The word consuming pictures the fire burning to nothing everything it touches.
2:4: דָּרַךְ קַשְׁתּוֹ כְּאוֹיֵב נִצָּב יְמִינוֹ כְּצָר

The writer uses comparisons to describe God’s hostility toward his own people. He says that God has bent his bow like an enemy; his right hand is stationed like an adversary, meaning that God has prepared to attack his people the way an enemy would and has taken the stance of one ready to fight against them.
Here, his right hand represents God’s power and ability to act.

Here, the eye represents sight and what is pleasing to behold. The phrase the delights of the eye refers to everything people treasured and found beautiful. Some understand this as referring specifically to the fine young men of Judah.
The writer speaks of Zion as if it were a woman, calling it the daughter of Zion, and he describes the city as her tent or dwelling place. For more information, see the Lamentations 2 Introduction.
The writer uses a comparison to describe God’s anger. He says that God has poured out his anger like fire, meaning that God’s anger has been destructive and consuming.
2:5: The writer uses a comparison to describe how God has treated his own people. He says that The Lord has become like an enemy, meaning that God has acted against his people as an enemy would.
בִּלַּע יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּלַּע כָּל־אַרְמְנוֹתֶיהָ שִׁחֵת מִבְצָרָיו

These three phrases mean basically the same thing. Each one emphasizes the totality of God’s destruction by repeating the same idea with different words. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with words that show that the second and third phrases are repeating the first one, not saying something additional.
The writer is speaking of God’s destruction of Israel as if God had swallowed the nation like a beast consuming its prey. This emphasizes the completeness of the destruction.
The terms mourning and groaning mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together for emphasis.
2:6: The writer is comparing God’s destruction of his sanctuary to the tearing down of his garden booth, a temporary seasonal shelter.
The writer is referring to all of Israel’s sacred worship occasions by naming two major components, appointed festival and Sabbath.
The writer is referring to all of Israel’s leadership by naming two major components, king and priest.
2:7: Here, his altar represents the entire sacrificial worship system of Israel.
Here, the hand of the enemy represents the power and control of the enemy.
The writer compares the shouts of the enemies in the house of the Lord to the shouts of worshipers on an appointed festival day.
2:8: The writer is speaking of God’s careful planning for destruction as if God had stretched out the measuring line like a builder measuring before construction. However, God measured not to build but to tear down.
The writer is speaking of God’s destructive action as if God were swallowing up the city, consuming it completely. The phrase his hand represents God’s active power.
The writer speaks of the rampart and wall as if they were people who could mourn and languish. He says this because they lie in ruins.
The writer is referring to all of Jerusalem’s defensive structures by naming two major components, the rampart and the wall.
2:9: The writer is speaking of the complete destruction of Her gates as if they had sunk into the ground.
The terms destroyed and shattered mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here, law represents the entire instruction and guidance of God. Without their land and temple, the people have no access to God’s teaching.
The writer is speaking of receiving a vision from the Lord as if it were something that could be found through searching. He means that the Lord has ceased communicating with the prophets.
2:10: Sitting on the ground in silence, throwing up dust on their heads, and putting on sackcloth (rough goat-hair cloth) were mourning customs expressing grief too deep for words. Bowing the head to the ground was a symbolic action expressing utter humiliation and grief.
The writer is referring to all of the people of Jerusalem by naming two extremes, the elders (the oldest) and The virgins (the youngest women).
2:11: The writer is using the expression My eyes have failed with tears as a common expression of the culture to mean that one has wept so much that the eyes are exhausted and can no longer produce tears.
Here, my inner parts represent deep emotional anguish. Jeremiah uses the internal organs as a way of referring to intense grief.
The writer is speaking of his emotional anguish as if his liver had been poured out to the ground, like liquid spilling from a container. He means that he is completely overwhelmed.
The terms child and infant are paired to represent the very youngest and most vulnerable members of the community.
2:12: The writer compares the children to the slain collapsing in the streets, meaning the children fall as though they have been mortally wounded, but from hunger rather than the sword.
The writer is speaking of the children’s lives slowly draining away as if their souls were poured out like liquid from a container. He means that the children die slowly in their mothers’ arms.
2:13: The writer uses a series of rhetorical questions to express the idea that he cannot find anything adequate to say about Jerusalem’s suffering, to express the idea that nothing compares to her suffering, and that no comparison is adequate to bring comfort.
The writer uses a comparison to describe Jerusalem’s destruction. He compares it to the greatness of the sea, meaning that the brokenness is immeasurable and overwhelming in its vastness.
The writer uses another rhetorical question to express the idea that no one can remedy Jerusalem’s suffering.
2:14: The terms falsehood and worthlessness mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together to emphasize that what the prophets claimed to see had no truth or value.
The terms falsehood and enticement are paired to characterize the prophets’ deceptive messages as both untrue and misleadingly appealing.
2:15: Clapping hands at someone was a symbolic action by which they showed scorn, mockery, and contempt. This is not applause.
Hissing and shaking the head were symbolic gestures of derision and scorn.
הֲזֹאת הָעִיר שֶׁיֹּאמְרוּ כְּלִילַת יֹפִי מָשׂוֹשׂ לְכָל־הָאָרֶץ
The passers-by use a rhetorical question to express their disbelief that the once-glorious city has fallen to such ruin.
The expressions the perfection of beauty and the joy of all the earth are paired to express the former glory of Jerusalem.
2:16: Opening the mouth wide against someone was a symbolic action by which someone showed hostility, scorn, and readiness to devour.
Hissing and gnashing the teeth were symbolic gestures expressing hatred, rage, and contempt.
The enemies are speaking of their destruction of Jerusalem as if they had swallowed her up like an animal consuming its prey.

The expressions we have found and we have seen mean similar things. The enemies are using the two expressions together to express their satisfaction at finally witnessing the destruction they longed for.
2:17: The writer is speaking of God increasing the power of the enemies as if he had lifted up their horn, since a horn represents the strength of a powerful animal.
2:18: The writer speaks of the wall of the daughter of Zion as if it were a person who could weep. He says this because the wall lies in ruins and he urges it to mourn.
The writer uses a comparison to describe how abundant and continuous the weeping should be. He compares the flow of tears to a river, meaning the weeping should be constant and unceasing.
The writer is referring to all the time without stopping by naming two extremes, day and night.
The expression the daughter of your eye was a common expression meaning the pupil of the eye. In this context it means that one should not let the eyes stop weeping.
2:19: The writer assumes that his readers will know that the night watches were the periods into which the night was divided for keeping guard.
שִׁפְכִי כַמַּיִם לִבֵּךְ נֹכַח פְּנֵי אֲדֹנָי

The writer uses a comparison to describe complete, unreserved prayer. He compares pouring out the heart to pouring out water, meaning one should hold nothing back and empty oneself completely before God.
Here, the face of the Lord represents God’s presence.
Here, lift up your hands represents the act of praying and pleading with God.
By the expression at the head of every street, the writer means that children are fainting from hunger everywhere.
2:20: The writer uses rhetorical questions to express grief that God would allow his own people to suffer so terribly, to express outrage that women have been driven to eat their own children, and to express shock that religious leaders have been killed in the very place that was meant to be holy and safe.
The expression their fruit was a common expression meaning their children or offspring.
The writer is referring to all of Israel’s religious leaders by naming two representative roles, priest and prophet.
2:21: The writer is referring to people of every age by naming two extremes, Young and old.
Jeremiah is referring to all the young people of the community by naming both groups, my young women and my young men.
The expression have fallen by the sword was a common expression meaning to be killed in battle.
The writer is using the expression on the day of your anger to refer to the specific time when God executed judgment.
2:22: The point of this comparison is that just as guests are invited to an appointed festival, so has God summoned numerous terrors from all around.
The writer is using the expression the day of the anger of the Lord to refer to the time of divine judgment.
The terms an escapee and a survivor mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together to emphasize that absolutely no one got away.
The terms carried and multiplied are paired to express the full cycle of motherhood, both bearing and nurturing children. The writer speaks as a mother figure who carried and raised these people.
The writer is speaking of the enemy’s total destruction of the people as if the enemy had consumed them like food.
3:1: The writer is speaking of the experience of affliction as if it were something he could see.
Here the writer is speaking of God’s punishment as if it were a rod used to strike someone.
3:2: Here the writer is speaking of suffering as if it were darkness and of well-being as if it were light.
3:3: Here, his hand represents God’s power and action.
The writer is saying all the day as a generalization for emphasis.
3:4: The terms my flesh and my skin mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:5: Here the writer is speaking of God’s opposition as if God built siege works against him and surrounded him like an army besieging a city.
The terms poison and hardship mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:6: Here the writer is speaking as if God had placed him in dark places, the realm where the forgotten dead dwell without hope.
The point of this comparison is that just as the dead of long ago are forgotten and have no hope, so the writer feels completely hopeless, as though no one remembers him.
3:7: By He walled me in, and I cannot go out, the writer means that God caused him to be imprisoned so that he could not leave (see Jeremiah 37:15–16).
By he made my chains heavy, the writer means that God caused him to be bound in heavy chains (see Jeremiah 40:1).
3:8: The terms I cry out and call for help mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here the writer is speaking of his prayer as if it were a physical object that God shuts out or blocks.
3:9: Here the writer is speaking of his life direction as if it were a way or path, and of God blocking his progress as if God had walled up those ways with hewn stone.
Here the writer is speaking of his life direction as if it were paths, and of God confusing his plans as if God had made those paths crooked.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
3:10: Here the writer is speaking of God as if he were a bear lying in ambush.
דֹּב אֹרֵב הוּא לִי אריה בְּמִסְתָּרִים
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here the writer is speaking of God as if he were a lion in hiding places.
3:11: Here the writer is speaking of his life as if it were paths or ways that God turned aside.
3:12: Here the writer is speaking of God as if he were an archer who bent his bow and aimed at him as a target.
The point of this comparison is that just as a target is set up to be struck by arrows, so God has set the writer up to receive his arrows of affliction.
3:13: Here the writer is speaking of God’s affliction as if God were an archer whose arrows pierced his kidneys, representing deep inner pain.
The writer is speaking of the arrows as if they were sons of his quiver.
3:14: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here the writer is speaking of becoming an object of ridicule as if he literally became a laughingstock.
The writer is saying all my people as a generalization for emphasis.
3:15: The writer is speaking of God imposing bitter suffering on him as if God had literally filled him with bitter herbs and saturated him with wormwood.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here, wormwood refers to a plant that tastes very bitter.
3:16: Here the writer is speaking of his degrading humiliation as if God had literally made his teeth grind on gravel.
The writer is speaking of being brought low in mourning and shame as if God had literally pressed him down in the ashes.
3:18: Here the writer is speaking of his endurance and hope as if they were living things that could perish.
3:19: The terms my affliction and my wandering mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together for emphasis.
The terms the wormwood and the poison mean similar things.
Here the writer speaks of his bitter suffering as if it were wormwood and poison that he was forced to taste.
3:20: The writer speaks of his soul as if it were a person who bows down.
3:21: Here, This refers forward to what the writer is about to say, not back to what he has just described.
Here the heart represents where the writer’s thoughts and emotions exist. He is speaking of recalling something as if he were physically bringing it back to his heart.
3:22: Many ancient manuscripts read for we have not been consumed, with the writer and the people as the subject. Other ancient manuscripts read “his steadfast love has not ceased,” with the steadfast love of the Lord as the subject.
3:24: Here the writer is speaking of the Lord as if he were an inherited portion of land.
Here, my soul represents the writer himself from the perspective of his inner being.
3:25: Here, the soul represents the person who seeks God.
3:27: Here the writer is speaking of discipline and suffering as if they were a yoke placed on a person’s shoulders.
3:28: The writer is using the third-person imperative form Let him sit to give instruction about what a person should do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team here and elsewhere in this lament.
3:29: In the writer’s culture, putting one’s mouth in the dust was a symbolic action that signified extreme humility and submission before God.
3:30: In the writer’s culture, giving one’s cheek to the one striking him was a symbolic action that signified patient acceptance of suffering and willingness to endure insult without retaliation.
3:33: Here the heart represents God’s true desire and will. The writer is saying that God does not afflict people because he desires to do so.
3:34: Here, under his feet represents dominion and oppressive power.
3:35: Here, before the face of the Most High represents being in the presence of the Most High.
3:36: The writer is speaking of acting unjustly toward someone as if it were physically twisting or distorting him, using the same image as “turn aside” in the previous verse.
This could mean: (1) that the Lord does not regard with approval the wrong actions described in verses 34–36; or (2) that the author is using the question form for emphasis.
3:37: מִי זֶה אָמַר וַתֶּהִי אֲדֹנָי לֹא צִוָּה
The writer is using these questions to emphasize that no one can speak something into existence apart from God.
3:38: Here, the mouth of the Most High represents the decrees and commands of God.
Jeremiah is referring to everything that happens by naming two extremes, the evil things and the good.
3:40: Here the writer is speaking of examining conduct and behavior as if it were ways or paths that a person could search.
The terms search and examine mean similar things. Jeremiah is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:41: Here the heart represents the inner being and affections. The writer is speaking of directing his heart toward God as if it were something he could lift up.
Here, hands represents the gesture of prayer.
3:42: The terms transgressed and rebelled mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:43: Here the writer is speaking of God’s nose as if it were a garment that God covered himself with. The nose refers to anger.
3:44: Here the writer is speaking of a barrier to communication with God as if God had covered himself in a cloud.
Here the writer is speaking of prayer as if it were a physical object that could be blocked from traveling through a barrier.
3:45: Here the writer is speaking of the people as if they were offscouring and refuse, that is, filth and garbage that others discard.
The terms Offscouring and refuse mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:47: פַּחַד וָפַחַת הָיָה לָנוּ הַשֵּׁאת וְהַשָּׁבֶר
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
The terms Terror and the pit mean similar things. Also, the terms the desolation and the destruction mean similar things. The writer is using two terms together for emphasis.
3:48: The writer says Streams of water go down from my eye as an extreme statement for emphasis.
Here, my eye represents the writer himself as the one who is weeping.
Here the writer is speaking of his people as if they were a daughter.
3:49: The writer speaks of his eye as if it were a person who could pour out tears on its own.
The writer says does not cease, without stopping as an overstatement for emphasis.
3:51: The writer is using the term eye to mean what he sees.
Here, my soul represents the writer himself from the perspective of his inner being.
Here the writer is speaking of the women of his city as the daughters of my city.
3:52: The point of this comparison is that just as a bird is helpless and easily caught by hunters, so the writer’s enemies pursued him relentlessly.
3:53: By They silenced my life in the pit, the writer means that his enemies threw him into a cistern intending to kill him (see Jeremiah 38:6).
3:54: By Waters flowed over my head, the writer means that water in the cistern rose up around him and he was in danger of drowning (see Jeremiah 38:6).
The expression I am cut off was a common expression meaning I am about to die or I am separated from the living.
3:55: Here, your name represents God himself and his character.
By the pit of the depths, Jeremiah means the deepest part of the cistern where his enemies had thrown him (see Jeremiah 38:6).
3:56: Here, my voice represents the words the writer spoke in prayer.
Here, your ear represents God’s hearing and attention.
The terms my relief and my cry for help mean similar things. The writer is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:58: Here the writer is speaking of God defending him as if God were a legal advocate who pleaded his cases in a courtroom.
Here, my soul represents the writer himself.
3:62: Here, the lips of those rising against me represents the hostile speech of the writer’s enemies.
3:63: The writer is referring to everything his enemies do by naming two major components, their sitting and their rising.
3:64: Here, their hands represents the actions and deeds of the writer’s enemies.
3:65: The expression a covering of heart was a common expression meaning spiritual stubbornness or obstinacy of mind.
3:66: The writer is using the phrase in nose as a common expression of the culture to mean in anger.
Here the writer is speaking of the realm of the living as being under the heavens of the Lord.
4:1: The word How introduces an exclamation of sorrow which expresses strong feelings of shock and grief at the way the people of Zion are now treated. This is poetic language and begins the lament for the destruction of Jerusalem and its people.
Here the writer is speaking as if the people of Jerusalem were gold that has lost its luster and fine gold that has been altered.
Here the writer is speaking as if the people of the city were The stones of holiness and liquid that has been poured out and scattered.
The writer is using at the head of every street as a common expression of the culture to mean at the beginning or top of every street.
4:2: Here the writer is speaking as if the people of Jerusalem were precious metal that could be weighed against fine gold.
The point of this comparison is that just as jars of clay are cheap and easily broken, so the sons of Zion are now treated as worthless.
4:3: The writer is speaking of the daughter of my people as if the people group were one woman.
The point of this comparison is that just as ostriches in the wilderness abandon their eggs and neglect their young, so the people have become cruel to their children.
4:4: Here, the writer is speaking of the top of the infant’s mouth as if it were a roof.
4:6: Here, iniquity could represent: (1) the sin itself, meaning the sinfulness of the people is worse than the sinfulness of Sodom; or (2) the punishment for sin, meaning God has punished the people more severely than he punished Sodom.

This could mean: (1) no one expressed grief for Sodom, that is, no one wrung their hands in anguish over its destruction; or (2) no human hands were involved in its destruction because God destroyed it suddenly.
4:7: This could mean: (1) Nazirites refers to people who had taken a special vow of dedication to God, as described in Numbers 6:1–21. Their pure appearance would reflect their consecrated life; or (2) the word refers more generally to nobles, leaders, or people who were set apart by their high position.
The point of this comparison is that just as snow and milk are bright and clean, so the Nazirites had a pure appearance.
The point of this comparison is that just as corals have a rich red color and sapphire is very precious, so the Nazirites’ bodies had a healthy, ruddy complexion and fine form.
4:8: The point of this comparison is that just as soot is very dark, so the appearance of the people has become extremely dark because of starvation and suffering.
The point of this comparison is that just as wood is dry and lifeless, so the skin of the starving people has become dried out.
4:9: Here, the slain of the sword represents those who died in battle.

Jeremiah uses three phrases that build on each other to express the same idea with increasing intensity. The writer is speaking to the people of Edom, who are not present. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the judgment that will come on Edom as well.

The writer actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. He is not genuinely urging Edom to celebrate but is sarcastically warning that judgment is coming for them as well.
